newsitem.title: USA: US junk bond fund cash flows turn negative-AMG.
newsitem.headline: US junk bond fund cash flows turn negative-AMG.

text.p: Investors pulled money out of U.S. high-yield bond mutual funds in the latest week, causing cash flow figures to turn negative for the first time since May 28, according to AMG Data Services.
AMG reported net cash outflows of $25.2 million for the week ended August 13.
The last time the weekly figure was negative was the week ended May 28, when the mutual fund tracking company reported net outflows of $31.6 million from U.S. junk funds.

Sam DeRosa-Farag, head of high-yield bond strategy at Donaldson Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp, said the recent sell-off in the Treasury market was the most likely cause of the reversal in junk bond cash flows.
"What you see is a pattern in which the high-yield market is very sensitive to interest rates and the interest rate outlook," he added.

"As soon as you have serious Treasury volatility, you find that all other instruments such as high-yield bonds and equities will start to experience above average volatility, with comparable uncertainty," he said.
Investors pulled a total of $889 million out of U.S. equity funds this week, the highest amount for the entire year, said Robert Adler, president of AMG.
"Most of the (stock fund) redemptions occurred in the small cap sector. High-yield investors seem to operate in tandem with investors in more aggressive stock funds," he said.
Adler added that high-yield redemptions may also have been affected by recent weakness in emerging market funds.
"Funds that invest in Asian securities have had net redemptions in each of that last six weeks, " he said.
"Although redemptions are not accelerating, there may be some sympathy (among junk bond investors) to the weaker performance of the emerging markets," he said.
In comparison to junk funds, Treasury bond funds also experienced small redemptions this week, while investment-grade corporate bond funds saw slight inflows, he said.

"Typically withdrawals from high-yield funds are not limited to a single week. It remains to be seen if (high-yield) investors continue to withdraw money if the (Treasury) market stablizes," said Adler.

AMG's figures for high-yield cash flows are tallied from junk bonds funds that report on a weekly basis only. The data also excludes reinvested distribution, therefore representing only net new money coming into the funds.

Mutual fund cash flows are closely watched by junk bond players becuase the high-yield bond market has one of the heaviest concentrations of mutual fund money of any major financial asset class in the U.S.
